cli-0.summary: Create your own copy of Tailspin Toys from the template and start a codespace. Its terminal is where you'll install and run Copilot CLI.
concepts: Creating a repository from the template also seeds a backlog of GitHub issues you'll work from.
A codespace (or the same dev container locally) ships every prerequisite, so everyone starts from an identical environment.
Note your repository path (owner/repo); later lessons refer to it.

questions.q: Where does the backlog of issues you work from come from?
options: The template creates it automatically with your repository
You file the issues yourself in the next exercise
Copilot CLI generates them the first time it starts
They're copied from pull requests in the github-samples repository
questions.why: Creating the repository from the template seeds the backlog for you; there's nothing to file.

questions.q: Why does the workshop run in a codespace or dev container?
options: It has every prerequisite pre-installed, so the environment is consistent
Copilot CLI only runs inside a browser
Astro can't run on a local machine
A codespace is required to sign in to GitHub
questions.why: Both give a known-good environment. Locally, Reopen in Container builds the same dev container the codespace uses.

cli-1.summary: Install Copilot CLI with npm, sign in with a device code, trust the workshop folder and confirm Copilot answers a first question.
concepts: Copilot CLI needs Node.js 22 or newer; install it with npm install -g @github/copilot (WinGet and Homebrew also work).
On first launch you authenticate with a device code in the browser; in a codespace you may already be signed in.
Folder trust controls file access: trust once, remember the folder, or exit.
/help lists every slash command and keyboard shortcut.

questions.q: Which command does the lesson use to install Copilot CLI in the codespace?
questions.why: Codespaces come with Node.js, so the lesson installs the CLI globally with npm.

questions.q: What's the minimum Node.js version Copilot CLI needs?
questions.why: node --version should report v22.x.x or higher.

questions.q: Which trust option does the lesson pick for the workshop repository?
options: Yes, and remember this folder for future sessions
Trust all folders on this machine
questions.why: You'll work in this repository throughout, so remembering the folder avoids being asked again.

cli-2.summary: See how repository and path-scoped instruction files shape what Copilot writes. You generate a publishers helper, add a TSDoc standard, then regenerate and watch the code follow it.
concepts: .github/copilot-instructions.md is sent with every request; keep it to project-level context and global standards.
.github/instructions/*.instructions.md files target file types or tasks through an applyTo glob.
Instruction files can link to other files; those paths are relative to the instruction file, not the repo root.
Copilot is non-deterministic: judge the trend after an instruction change, not character-for-character output.
Copilot also reads AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md, and /init in the CLI can scaffold instructions.

questions.q: Which file is sent to Copilot with every request in the repository?
questions.why: The repository-level instructions file applies to every chat, CLI and cloud agent request.

questions.q: What does the applyTo field at the top of a *.instructions.md file do?
options: Sets a glob that decides which files the instructions apply to
Lists the agents allowed to read the file
Picks the branch the instructions apply to
Marks the file as required for every request
questions.why: unit-tests.instructions.md, for example, applies to TypeScript test files such as **/*.test.ts.

questions.q: A link inside drizzle.instructions.md points to another file. What is that path relative to?
questions.why: Paths in instruction files resolve from the instruction file's own location.

questions.q: After you add the TSDoc rule, one regenerated function still lacks a doc comment. What's the right conclusion?
options: Copilot is non-deterministic; look at the overall trend and tighten the wording if needed
The instructions file is being ignored and must be deleted
Instructions only apply after the codespace restarts
Instructions only affect inline code completions
questions.why: The lesson warns that output varies; the point is the consistent shift after the instruction change.

questions.q: Which Copilot CLI command can generate instruction files for you?
questions.why: Each surface has its own way; in Copilot CLI it's /init.

cli-3.summary: Use /plan to have Copilot read the filtering issue and draft a plan, refine it, let it build in autopilot, then review every change with /diff.
concepts: Start the session with copilot --yolo --enable-all-github-mcp-tools; add --continue to resume your last session.
--yolo allows all tools, paths and URLs. Use it only in an isolated environment such as a codespace or VM, and never alias it for daily work.
Plan mode asks clarifying questions and lays out the work, so the generated code better matches the requirements.
Autopilot works through each step without waiting for input until it judges the task complete.
All AI-generated code is reviewed before merge; /diff shows every changed file.

questions.q: What does the --yolo flag turn on?
options: Full automatic permissions: all tools, all paths and all URLs
questions.why: --yolo is shorthand for --allow-all-tools, --allow-all-paths and --allow-all-urls.

questions.q: Where is it appropriate to run Copilot CLI with --yolo?
options: Only in an isolated environment like a codespace or VM
As your default alias for everyday work
Anywhere, as long as you're on the main branch
Anywhere, because every action can be undone
questions.why: Full permissions are only safe where the blast radius is contained.

questions.q: Why begin the filtering work with /plan?
options: Copilot surfaces questions and gaps first, so the code better matches the requirements
It's the only way Copilot can read GitHub issues
It skips running the tests to save time
questions.why: Time spent planning helps Copilot generate code that matches what you asked for.

questions.q: Which command reviews the changes Copilot made, inside the CLI?
questions.why: /diff shows the changed files; arrow keys move between them.

questions.q: Put the CLI feature workflow in order.
items: Start a plan with /plan and point it at the issue
Review the plan and add feedback
Approve it and let Copilot build in autopilot
questions.why: Plan, refine, build, then review: the same order a careful developer follows.

cli-4.summary: Learn what MCP is, add the Playwright MCP server with /mcp add, start the app, and have Copilot drive a real browser to check the filtering feature.
concepts: MCP servers give agents tools (actions) and resources (up-to-date information) from outside the editor.
The GitHub MCP server is built in to Copilot CLI; Playwright is added as a second, local server.
Treat MCP servers like any dependency: review the source, verify the publisher, limit sensitive access.
--headless runs the browser without a window, which a codespace needs because it has no desktop.
/mcp add writes to ~/.copilot/mcp-config.json; /mcp show lists active servers.
Playwright MCP reads the page's accessibility tree, so a functional check doubles as a light accessibility check.

questions.q: In MCP, how do tools differ from resources?
options: Tools perform actions; resources provide up-to-date information
Resources perform actions; tools provide information
They're two names for MCP servers
questions.why: Agents read resources and call tools, both through an MCP server.

questions.q: Why is the Playwright server started with --headless in a codespace?
options: There's no desktop to display a browser window
It makes the tests run in parallel
questions.why: Headless mode runs the browser without a visible window.

questions.q: Where does /mcp add save the server configuration?
questions.why: Copilot CLI keeps MCP servers in your user-level config file.

questions.q: How does the Playwright MCP server understand a page?
options: From the raw HTML source only
questions.why: It reasons over labelled elements the way assistive technology does.

questions.q: Which MCP server works in Copilot CLI with no setup?
options: None; every server must be added
questions.why: That built-in server is how Copilot reads your backlog and opens PRs.

questions.q: Put the steps for testing with Playwright MCP in order.
items: Fill in name playwright, type Local, command npx @playwright/mcp@latest --headless
Start the app with npm run dev in a separate terminal
Ask Copilot to test the feature with the Playwright MCP server
questions.why: Register the server, confirm it, run the app, then ask for the test.

cli-5.summary: Explore the make-contribution skill, then ask Copilot to create a pull request. It loads the skill on its own and follows the team's PR rules.
concepts: A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md (name and description frontmatter) plus optional scripts and resources.
Skills live in .github/skills in a project or ~/.copilot/skills globally.
The agent loads a skill on demand by matching your request to its description, so write a clear, scenario-specific description.
Agent Skills is an open standard; the same skill works in VS Code agent mode, cloud agent, Copilot CLI and the Copilot app.

questions.q: How does Copilot decide which skill to use?
options: It matches your request against each skill's description
It runs skills in alphabetical order
You must always name the skill in your prompt
Every skill runs on every request
questions.why: A vague description is the difference between a skill that's used and one that's ignored.

questions.q: Which frontmatter does a SKILL.md need?
questions.why: The name identifies the skill and the description tells the agent when to use it.

questions.q: Where can skills live?
questions.why: Project skills are shared with the team; global ones follow you.

questions.q: Which skill handled "Can you please create a pull request for me!"?
questions.why: Its description covers commits, pushes and PRs, so it ran the tests, branched, committed and opened the PR.

cli-6.summary: Review the accessibility custom agent, select it with /agent, and have it implement a persisted high-contrast toggle with end-to-end tests and a PR.
concepts: Custom agents are Markdown files in .github/agents (or ~/.copilot/agents) with required name and description frontmatter.
A custom agent is the worker; skills are its tools.
Custom agents have their own context window and can orchestrate skills and other agents.
Teams use them to codify expertise: accessibility, security, testing.

questions.q: Which statement matches how the lesson separates custom agents and skills?
options: A custom agent is the worker; skills are tools it can use
A skill is the worker; agents are tools it can use
They're the same thing with different file names
Skills can call agents, but agents can't use skills
questions.why: The accessibility agent even used the PR skill when it opened its pull request.

questions.q: What frontmatter is required in a custom agent file?
questions.why: The lesson calls this out as required.

questions.q: How do you choose a custom agent in Copilot CLI?
questions.why: /agent lists the agents available to the session.

questions.q: Where are the project's custom agents defined?
questions.why: Global agents go in ~/.copilot/agents.

cli-7.summary: Share a session as a gist, inspect and compact the context window, switch models, and optionally hand work to cloud agent with /delegate.
concepts: /share creates a Markdown file or GitHub gist of the session, including prompts, skills and agents used.
/context shows System/Tools, Messages, Buffer and Free space.
Copilot compacts automatically near the limit. Use /clear for an unrelated task and /compact to choose when to compact.
/model lists models with their cost-per-request multiplier; the choice persists.
/delegate sends the session to cloud agent, which works asynchronously and opens a PR (all plans except Copilot Free).

questions.q: You're switching to an unrelated part of the app. Which command keeps old context from confusing Copilot?
questions.why: /clear starts fresh; /compact only summarizes.

questions.q: What does /compact do?
options: Summarizes the conversation history to free context space
Compresses the files in your repository
questions.why: It lets you control when compaction happens instead of waiting for the automatic one.

questions.q: In the /context view, what is the Buffer?
questions.why: System/Tools, Messages, Buffer and Free space make up the window.

questions.q: Where does /delegate send your session?
options: To Copilot cloud agent, which works asynchronously and opens a PR
questions.why: You keep working while cloud agent takes the longer task; track it at github.com/copilot/agents.

questions.q: Which plan can't use /delegate?
questions.why: Cloud agent is on every plan except Copilot Free.

cli-8.summary: Recap the CLI harness with a reference table of slash commands, the best practices that matter most, and where to go next.
concepts: Instruction files, custom agents and skills drive output quality; awesome-copilot has templates.
Context still matters: say what you want built, why, and how.
/plan, /review, /diff, /session, /usage and /add-dir round out the everyday commands.

questions.q: What does /plan <prompt> do?
options: Creates an implementation plan before coding
Schedules a prompt to run later
Shows your Copilot plan and billing
questions.why: It's the same plan mode you used for filtering.

questions.q: Which command adds a directory to Copilot's trusted list?
questions.why: Trust controls which folders Copilot can read and write.

questions.q: Besides instructions, agents and skills, what changes output quality the most?
options: Clearly describing what you want, why, and how
Always choosing the most expensive model
questions.why: If a piece of information would help Copilot, pass it along.

vscode-0.summary: Create your Tailspin Toys copy, start a codespace, and confirm GitHub Copilot Chat is installed and signed in.
concepts: The template seeds your backlog of issues automatically.
Codespaces include the Copilot Chat extension; elsewhere, install GitHub Copilot Chat from the Marketplace.
Send a first message in Copilot Chat to activate it, signing in if prompted.

questions.q: Copilot Chat isn't in your editor. What do you do?
options: Install GitHub Copilot Chat from the Extensions view or Marketplace
Recreate the repository from the template
questions.why: Codespaces usually have it already; otherwise install the extension and sign in.

questions.q: What should you record after creating the repository?
questions.why: Later exercises refer to your repository path.

vscode-1.summary: Learn instruction files in Copilot Chat: send a prompt, add a TSDoc standard, resend the same prompt, then have Copilot create and merge the PR for you.
concepts: In the IDE, instruction files apply to Copilot Chat code generation, not to completions or next-edit suggestions.
Repository instructions apply to every request; *.instructions.md files scope by applyTo glob.
Configure Chat → Generate Agent Instructions drafts instructions for you in VS Code.
Copilot can find the issue, open the PR and merge it with the GitHub tools wired into the template; you approve each action with Allow.

questions.q: In VS Code, where are instruction files used?
questions.why: The lesson notes they don't apply to completions or next-edit suggestions.

questions.q: Where in VS Code can Copilot draft instruction files for you?
questions.why: /init is the Copilot CLI equivalent.

questions.q: unit-tests.instructions.md has applyTo set for test files. Which file does it apply to?
questions.why: Its glob matches TypeScript test files such as **/*.test.ts.

questions.q: Why merge the instructions change to main before the next exercise?
options: The next exercise branches from main, so the new standard must be there
Copilot only reads instructions from tagged releases
Unmerged instruction files are deleted after 24 hours
VS Code can't open files on other branches
questions.why: Committing it to main means the updated guidance is in place for the agent-mode work.

vscode-2.summary: Run the site, have agent mode list and prioritize the backlog, attach the UI instructions, then build filtering across the data layer, UI and tests until everything passes.
concepts: Agent mode explores the project, edits multiple files, runs tasks like tests and fixes its own mistakes.
Agent mode works in your IDE with fast feedback; cloud agent works asynchronously through issues and PRs.
Tailspin Toys is one Astro app; pages query SQLite through Drizzle in their frontmatter, and helpers live in src/lib/.
Add Context → Instructions attaches a specific instructions file such as ui.
Review, then select Keep for all changes at the end; Continue approves commands the agent wants to run.

questions.q: How does agent mode differ from cloud agent?
options: Agent mode works in your IDE with quick feedback; cloud agent works asynchronously through issues and PRs
Agent mode only answers questions; cloud agent writes code
They're the same feature with two names
Cloud agent runs on your laptop; agent mode runs on GitHub
questions.why: Cloud agent acts like a peer programmer you hand issues to.

questions.q: How did you give Copilot the UI guidance for the filtering task?
options: Pasted the file into the prompt
questions.why: Attaching the instructions file adds its guidance and linked files to the request.

questions.q: When should you select Keep?
options: After the agent finishes and you've reviewed and tried the changes
On every edit as soon as it appears
questions.why: You get one Keep or Undo for all changes at the end; there's no need to click while work is in progress.

questions.q: Some tests fail while the agent works. What does that mean?
options: It's normal; the agent iterates between code and tests until they pass
The agent has crashed and must be restarted
questions.why: Agent mode goes back and forth until it detects no errors.

questions.q: Which describes the Tailspin Toys architecture?
options: A single Astro app querying SQLite through Drizzle
A React single-page app with an Express API
A Flask backend with an Astro frontend
questions.why: There's no separate backend API or client-side framework.

vscode-3.summary: Review .vscode/mcp.json, add the local Playwright server next to the remote GitHub server, test filtering in a browser, then publish the branch and have Copilot open the PR.
concepts: .vscode/mcp.json configures the workspace's MCP servers.
The github server is remote over HTTP (api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/); nothing is installed locally.
The playwright server is local: VS Code runs npx @playwright/mcp@latest --headless.
VS Code starts servers on demand and asks you to trust them first.
The Sparkle button in Source Control drafts the commit message.

questions.q: Which file configures MCP servers for this VS Code workspace?
questions.why: ~/.copilot/mcp-config.json is Copilot CLI's file.

questions.q: How does the github server in mcp.json run?
options: Remotely over HTTP, with nothing installed locally
As a separate VS Code extension
questions.why: You authenticate with GitHub the first time Copilot uses one of its tools.

questions.q: When does VS Code start an MCP server?
options: On demand, after you trust it, the first time Copilot needs its tools (or when you select Start)
Only after you restart VS Code
questions.why: Starting it by hand is optional.

questions.q: What drafts a commit message for you in Source Control?
questions.why: Copilot writes the message from the staged changes.

vscode-4.summary: Branch off main, review the accessibility custom agent, pick it from the agents dropdown, and ask it for a persisted high-contrast toggle.
concepts: VS Code lists every agent in .github/agents in the agents dropdown at the bottom of Chat.
Selecting a custom agent scopes the chat to its instructions and tooling.
Each edit appears inline with a diff; the Files changed indicator tracks the working set.
Keep accessibility work on its own branch, separate from the open filtering PR.

questions.q: Where do custom agents appear in VS Code?
options: In the agents dropdown at the bottom of the Chat view
In the Command Palette under Tasks
questions.why: The dropdown shows the active agent, default unless you pick another.

questions.q: Why create a fresh branch off main for the accessibility work?
options: To keep it separate from the filtering PR that's still open
Custom agents only work on new branches
main is locked during the workshop
VS Code requires one branch per agent
questions.why: Separate branches keep each PR focused and reviewable.

questions.q: True or false: custom agents have their own context window and can orchestrate skills and other agents.
questions.why: That's what makes them suited to larger, multi-step work.

vscode-5.summary: Watch the agent's tool calls, keep or undo each diff, then steer the same session to add light mode next to high contrast.
concepts: Chat shows each file read, edit and terminal command as it happens.
Keep accepts a diff; Undo reverts it so the agent can try again.
Commands that need permission pause on Allow; approve only what you're comfortable with.
Continuing the same session keeps the agent's context; Stop halts a wrong direction so you can clarify.

questions.q: Why add light mode in the same chat session instead of a new one?
options: The agent keeps context: components it touched, styling and the local-storage pattern
New chats can't use custom agents
Light mode needs high contrast to be undone first
questions.why: Steering an in-flight session is faster than starting over.

questions.q: The agent starts refactoring the toggle UI in a way you don't want. What do you do?
options: Select Stop, then send a clarifying follow-up
Wait and Undo everything at the end
questions.why: Stopping early saves time and keeps the useful work.

questions.q: What does Undo on an inline diff do?
options: Reverts that change so the agent can take another pass
questions.why: Keep and Undo act on individual edits.

vscode-6.summary: Publish the accessibility branch, open the pull request, review the files changed, approve workflows, and optionally tag @copilot for a second opinion.
concepts: AI doesn't change the fundamentals: everything goes through a real review cycle.
Check toggles, local-storage persistence, styling, ARIA attributes and keyboard navigation.
Workflows on the PR may wait for approval: select Approve and run workflows.
Tagging @copilot in a PR comment starts a new session to address it.

questions.q: The PR shows workflows waiting. What do you select?
questions.why: Workflows need a human to approve them before they run.

questions.q: What happens when you tag @copilot in a PR comment?
options: Copilot starts a new session to address the comment
questions.why: Ask it, for example, to review the PR for additional WCAG issues.

questions.q: Which is most important to check in the accessibility diff?
questions.why: The accessibility patterns from the custom agent should be visible in the code.

cloud-0.summary: Create your Tailspin Toys copy and start a codespace for editing instruction files and reviewing the cloud agent's work.
concepts: The repository comes from the tailspin-toys template.
In this harness the codespace is for editing instructions and checking out Copilot's branches; cloud agent works on GitHub.

questions.q: What is the codespace used for in the cloud agent harness?
options: Editing instruction files and reviewing what cloud agent produces
questions.why: Cloud agent runs in GitHub Actions, not in your codespace.

questions.q: Where do you create your copy of the lab repository from?
options: Clone and push the docs folder
questions.why: The template gives you every file the lab needs.

cloud-1.summary: Review the repository's instruction files and add the TSDoc standard, then merge it to main so cloud agent reads it when you assign issues.
concepts: There's no before/after prompt here: cloud agent works asynchronously, so you see the effect later in its PRs.
Cloud agent reads instruction files from the branch the issue targets and branches from main.
Copilot also supports AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md.

questions.q: Why must the instructions change land on main?
options: Cloud agent branches from main and reads instructions from that branch
Instructions on other branches are ignored by every Copilot surface
GitHub deletes unmerged branches after a day
main is the only branch codespaces can push to
questions.why: Your assigned issues start from main, so the standard has to be there.

questions.q: Why doesn't this harness compare output before and after the instruction change?
options: Cloud agent works asynchronously on issues, so the effect shows later in its PRs
The comparison needs a paid plan
questions.why: You'll spot the TSDoc comments when you review the PRs.

questions.q: True or false: Copilot also reads instruction files written to other standards, such as AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md.
questions.why: Copilot supports several instruction-file conventions.

cloud-2.summary: Learn how cloud agent works, review copilot-setup-steps.yml, then file two issues (documentation and related games) and assign both to Copilot.
concepts: Assigning an issue makes Copilot open a draft [WIP] PR, set up its environment, post a to-do list and start working.
Its environment runs in GitHub Actions, customized by .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml.
That workflow has one job named copilot-setup-steps, and workflow_dispatch lets you test it from the Actions tab.
Scope issues clearly: there's no magic, and you don't get to skip the thinking.
A 👀 reaction on the issue means Copilot picked it up; View session shows its live work.

questions.q: Where does cloud agent's working environment run?
questions.why: That's why setup is defined as a workflow.

questions.q: Which file customizes the agent's environment?
questions.why: It installs Node, dependencies, Playwright browsers and seeds the database.

questions.q: Why does the setup workflow include a workflow_dispatch trigger?
options: So you can run it by hand from the Actions tab to test it
So it runs on every push
So it only runs on main
questions.why: You can check it works without waiting for Copilot to run it.

questions.q: What must the setup workflow's single job be called?
questions.why: Copilot looks for that job and runs it before it starts working.

questions.q: Put the cloud agent assignment flow in order.
items: Create an issue with a clear title and description
Copilot opens a draft [WIP] pull request
Select View session to watch it work
questions.why: Then you return to review once it's ready.

cloud-3.summary: Review the accessibility custom agent, then file a high-contrast issue and assign it to Copilot with the Accessibility agent selected.
concepts: Custom agents are Markdown files in .github/agents (or ~/.copilot/agents) with required name and description.
The Assign to Copilot dialog lets you pick a custom agent for the issue.
A custom agent is the worker; skills are its tools.

questions.q: How do you have a custom agent work an issue?
options: Pick it from the custom agents list in the Assign to Copilot dialog
Mention the agent's file name in the issue title
Add a label named after the agent
questions.why: Select Accessibility agent, then Assign.

questions.q: Where can custom agents be defined globally rather than per project?
questions.why: Project agents live in .github/agents.

cloud-4.summary: Use the agents page as mission control to watch every task, then steer the high-contrast session so it adds light mode too.
concepts: github.com/copilot/agents lists all agent tasks with open PRs.
Each session shows its steps: checkout, environment setup, MCP setup and the work itself, with a PR pane on the right.
Steer a running session from the Steer active session box; Copilot applies it after its current step.

questions.q: Where is the agents page?
questions.why: It's mission control for every cloud agent task.

questions.q: When does Copilot act on a steering message you send mid-session?
options: After it finishes the step it's working on
Only after the PR is merged
Never; you must assign a new issue
questions.why: It folds your request into its flow at the next step.

questions.q: What does the pane on the right of a selected session show?
options: The pull request and its files changed
questions.why: It's there for extra monitoring while the agent works.

cloud-5.summary: Review the three cloud agent PRs, approve workflows, request changes by tagging @copilot, and check out branches to test locally.
concepts: Copilot has read access to the repository and write access only to its own branch.
It works in an ephemeral GitHub Actions environment, and its workflows need human approval.
External access, MCP servers included, is limited by a firewall by default; the warning in the PR is expected.
Tag @copilot in a PR or inline comment and it starts a new session to address it.
Mark the draft PR ready and merge once you're happy.

questions.q: What can cloud agent write to?
options: Only the branch it uses for its work
questions.why: It has read access to the repository and write access to its own branch only.

questions.q: A PR shows a warning that Copilot was blocked by a firewall. What does it mean?
options: It's expected: external access is limited by default and can be customized
The PR is unsafe and must be closed
questions.why: The firewall is a guardrail, not a failure.

questions.q: How do you ask cloud agent to change its PR?
options: Close the PR and file a new issue
questions.why: Copilot sees the comment and starts a new session, then pushes a new commit.

questions.q: Workflows on Copilot's PR are waiting. Why?
options: Workflows on its PRs need human approval before they run
Copilot can't trigger Actions at all
The PR is still a draft
questions.why: Select Approve and run workflows after reviewing.

app-0.summary: Install Node.js 22 or newer (or use the dev container) and create your own copy of Tailspin Toys from the template.
concepts: Node.js is the only runtime the project needs; the LTS release is a safe choice.
With Docker you can use the dev container instead of installing Node locally.
The template seeds a backlog of issues in your new repository.

questions.q: Which Node.js version does the project need?
options: Node isn't needed for the app harness
questions.why: Agents run the test suite locally, which needs Node 22+.

questions.q: What's the alternative to installing Node.js on your machine?
options: The repository's dev container, if you have Docker
Using the Copilot app's built-in Node
questions.why: The dev container bundles Node for you; you don't need both.

app-1.summary: Install the GitHub Copilot app, sign in, add your repository, find your way around Sessions, Quick chats, My work and Automations, and ask a first quick chat.
concepts: The app is built on Copilot CLI and integrates natively with GitHub.
It needs Copilot Student or a paid plan; Business and Enterprise admins must enable the Copilot CLI policy.
Sessions each run in an isolated git worktree, so several agents can work in parallel.
Quick chats need no branch or worktree; My work shows issues and PRs for repositories you've added.

questions.q: What's the difference between a quick chat and a session?
options: Quick chats need no branch or worktree; sessions get their own isolated workspace
Quick chats can edit files; sessions can't
questions.why: Use quick chats for fast, throwaway questions.

questions.q: You're on Copilot Business and the app won't work. What does your admin need to do?
questions.why: The app is built on Copilot CLI, so the CLI policy must be on.

questions.q: What lets you run several agent sessions without their changes colliding?
options: Each session runs in its own git worktree
Sessions take turns on one branch
The app locks files while a session edits them
questions.why: Isolated worktrees keep parallel work apart.

questions.q: Where do your issues and pull requests appear in the app?
questions.why: It's filtered to repositories you've added to the app.

app-2.summary: Start your first session to show star ratings on the game cards, review the diff, run the app, then create and merge your first PR.
concepts: A session is a conversation, the agent's tool activity, and the list of changed files with diffs.
Every session gets a dedicated worktree and branch.
Naming the file to change isn't required, but it speeds Copilot up and reduces token use.
Toggle review panel opens the diff; the panel also has a built-in terminal.
Create PR turns into Ready to merge once the workflows pass.

questions.q: Why did the prompt name src/components/GameCard.astro?
options: It points Copilot to the right place, which is faster and uses fewer tokens
Copilot can't find files unless you name them
The app only edits files named in the prompt
It's needed to create the worktree
questions.why: Specifying files is optional but helpful.

questions.q: What three things do you see inside a session?
options: The conversation, the agent's tool activity, and the changed files
The issue, the PR and the CI logs
questions.why: That's the anatomy of a session.

questions.q: Which button label tells you the PR can be merged?
questions.why: The app watches the workflows and switches the button when they're done.

questions.q: What should a card show when starRating is null?
questions.why: The prompt asks for that text explicitly.

app-3.summary: Start a session from the coding-standards issue, have the agent update the instruction files, preview the code it would now write, then merge.
concepts: Most work starts from an issue: open it in My work and select New session.
Copilot reads AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md and GEMINI.md as well as its own instruction files.
Instruction files have a big impact, so have Copilot draft them and then review the result yourself.
Once merged to the default branch, the standard applies to every new session.

questions.q: How do you start a session from an issue?
options: Open the issue in My work, then select New session
Paste the issue URL into a quick chat
Assign the issue to yourself on github.com
questions.why: The issue is then already in the session's context.

questions.q: Which instruction standards does Copilot read besides its own files?
questions.why: So Copilot gets the right context whichever convention a repo uses.

questions.q: Why ask Copilot to show example code without making changes?
options: To see how the new instructions will shape generated code before you merge
Because the app can't write code in this lesson
questions.why: It's a quick check that the wording does what you intended.

questions.q: Why merge the standard to the default branch?
options: New sessions start from it, so every future session follows the standard
It's required to close the issue
questions.why: You'll see the effect in the next lesson's filtering code.

app-4.summary: From the filtering issue, plan in Plan mode, build in Autopilot, check the documentation standard was followed, and verify with /quality-checks.
concepts: Session modes: Interactive (works with you), Plan (plan first, you approve), Autopilot (fully autonomous).
Shift+Tab cycles the mode; you can change it at any time.
AI agents don't change the development process: issue, plan, build, test, validate, PR, merge.
The quality-checks skill runs unit tests, Playwright end-to-end tests and ESLint the team's way.

questions.q: Which mode writes code, runs tests and iterates without waiting for you?
questions.why: Save Autopilot for well-scoped, isolated tasks.

questions.q: How do you switch the session mode from the keyboard?
questions.why: Press it until the mode shows Plan.

questions.q: What does the quality-checks skill run?
options: Unit tests, Playwright end-to-end tests and ESLint
questions.why: It documents which script runs which suite, in what order, and how to debug failures.

questions.q: Put the development flow from the lesson in order.
items: Merge after review and CI pass
questions.why: AI-generated code goes through the same vetting as code written by hand.

app-5.summary: Add the Playwright MCP server from the app's catalog, then have the agent start the dev server and check filtering against the issue in a real browser.
concepts: Settings (Ctrl+,) → MCP servers has a catalog of popular servers.
Tests automate validation, but driving the real UI lets the agent react to what it sees.
Treat MCP servers as dependencies: review, verify, limit access.

questions.q: Where do you add an MCP server in the Copilot app?
questions.why: Search for Playwright and select Add server.

questions.q: What does browser validation add beyond the automated tests?
options: The agent uses the real UI like a user and can respond to problems it sees
It replaces the need for unit tests
It makes the tests run faster
questions.why: It gives more confidence the change behaves as expected.

questions.q: How should you treat an MCP server before using it?
options: Like any dependency: review its source and verify the publisher
As trusted, because it's in the catalog
As read-only, so it can't do harm
Ignore it; MCP servers can't access data
questions.why: Be cautious about granting access to sensitive resources.

app-6.summary: Turn on Agent Merge so the app creates the PR, watches CI and reviews, fixes what blocks it, and merges once everything is green.
concepts: Agent Merge fixes failing checks, responds to review comments, rebases when needed and merges when GitHub allows.
It runs in the background, survives app restarts and switches off once the PR is merged.
You still review and approve; the agent handles the mechanical finish line.
Enable it from the dropdown next to Create PR.

questions.q: With Agent Merge on, what is still your job?
questions.why: Agent Merge handles the mechanics, not the judgment.

questions.q: How do you turn on Agent Merge?
options: Open the dropdown next to Create PR and select Agent merge
Add an agent-merge label on github.com
questions.why: The button then changes to Agent merge.

questions.q: What happens to Agent Merge once the PR is merged?
options: It moves on to the next open PR
It deletes the repository branch protection
It stays on until you restart the app
questions.why: It's scoped to that one pull request.

app-7.summary: Create a Kanban triage canvas, save it to the repository with Agent Merge, and start work on an issue from it in a new session.
concepts: A canvas is a shared, interactive surface for a work artifact: a plan, board, checklist, dashboard or document.
Canvases are bidirectional: the agent updates them while you edit the same surface.
Use one when a task needs structure, iteration and verification that chat alone can't give.
Saving a canvas to the repository shares it with the team.

questions.q: What does "bidirectional" mean for a canvas?
options: Both you and the agent can edit the same surface
It works in light and dark mode
It can be opened on two machines
questions.why: The agent continues from your changes.

questions.q: When should you reach for a canvas instead of chat?
options: When the work needs structure, iteration and verification on an artifact
questions.why: Progress shows as visible changes to an artifact, not just chat replies.

questions.q: How did you share the triage canvas with the team?
options: Saved its definition to the repository and merged it
questions.why: Canvases become repository assets, like instruction files and skills.

app-8.summary: Create a manual, read-only automation, match mode and model to the task, and see what else the app offers.
concepts: Automations run agent tasks manually, on a schedule, or when an issue is created.
Keep scheduled automations scoped and non-destructive until you trust their output.
Plan to think, Interactive for focused changes, Autopilot only for well-scoped isolated tasks.
Also worth exploring: rubber duck, custom agents, /chronicle, bring your own key, cloud sandboxes and deep links.

questions.q: Which of these is not an automation trigger in the lesson?
options: When a pull request is merged
questions.why: The lesson lists Manual, On a schedule and When an issue is created.

questions.q: What's the advice for new scheduled automations?
options: Keep them scoped and non-destructive until you trust their output
Give them every tool so they never fail
questions.why: That's why the example prompt is read-only.

questions.q: When is Autopilot the right mode?
questions.why: Use Plan to think things through and Interactive to stay in the loop.

questions.q: What does /chronicle do?
options: Generates a narrative of what happened in a session
questions.why: Useful for sharing how work was done.
